text.p: Nigeria's military government has criticised groups urging army ruler General Sani Abacha to become an elected president next year, saying they were undermining its programme to restore democracy.

"These activities are clearly prejudicial to the integrity of the political transition programme of the federal government as well as the sincerity of its leadership in pursuit of its avowed commitment to handing over to a democratically-elected civilian administration in October 1998," said an official statement issued in the capital Abuja on Sunday night.
Newspapers have been awash with advertisements from groups calling on Abacha to shed his army uniform and stand as a candidate in next year's presidential election.
The lobby started after Abacha's press secretary David Atta said on national radio that Nigerians should put pressure on his boss to become an elected president.
Many opposition politicians believe the groups are sponsored by the authorities to facilitate a plot for Abacha to turn into an elected president as has happened often in West Africa.

The Abuja statement, signed by special duties minister Wada Nas, said people were free to express their views but that the activities of the lobbyists ... "can jeopardise the smooth implementation of the transition programme by government."

"The federal government reserves the right to deal appropriately with any form of threat to the smooth attainment of this onerous objective without prejudice to the rights and responsibilities of the majority of law-abiding and peace-loving Nigerians," it said.
Nigeria has been in political turmoil since the army annulled a presidential vote in 1993 presumed to have been won by wealthy businessman Moshood Abiola.

Abacha's transition-to-democracy programme is derided by the opposition as a charade because of the continued detention of Abiola and the non-registration of political parties formed by government opponents.
